name: Vichy France
info: The French State, the authoritarian rump state headed by Marshal Philippe Pétain from 1940 to 1944 after the German victory in the Battle of France, which collaborated with Nazi Germany, including in the deportation of Jews.

facts.capital: Vichy (seat of government; Paris nominally the capital); Sigmaringen in exile from September 1944
facts.founder: Marshal Philippe Pétain, voted full powers on 10 July 1940
facts.successor: The Provisional Government of the French Republic

t: On 10 July 1940 the National Assembly of the Third Republic voted by 569 to 80 to grant full powers to Pétain, whose regime called itself the French State.
Vichy took antisemitic measures of its own, such as the Law on the status of Jews of 3 October 1940, and its police organized the Vel' d'Hiv Roundup of July 1942.
In November 1942, after the Allies landed in French North Africa, German and Italian forces occupied all of Metropolitan France, ending any pretence of Vichy's independence.
dyk: Vichy replaced Marianne with Joan of Arc as the national symbol of France, and its "francisque" insignia arranged a Gallic baton and double-headed hatchet to resemble the fasces.
ev: Pétain signs the armistice with Germany
The National Assembly grants full powers to Pétain at Vichy
The Law on the status of Jews excludes Jews from the administration, the armed forces and many professions
Pétain and Hitler meet at Montoire, sealing state collaboration
French police arrest 13,152 Jews in the Vel' d'Hiv Roundup
The Allies land in French North Africa and the Axis occupies southern France in Case Anton
The French fleet is scuttled at Toulon to prevent its capture by the Axis
After the liberation of Paris, Pétain and his ministers are taken to Sigmaringen by German forces

sections.foundation:
France declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939, and after the Phoney War the Germans attacked in the West on 10 May 1940. As the French forces collapsed, Prime Minister Paul Reynaud wanted to continue the war from North Africa, but Vice-Premier Philippe Pétain and General Maxime Weygand insisted on an armistice. The government retreated to Bordeaux, Reynaud resigned, and President Albert Lebrun appointed the 84-year-old Pétain prime minister on 16 June 1940. The armistice with Germany was signed on 22 June.

Germany occupied northern France and the whole Atlantic coast and in effect annexed Alsace and Lorraine, leaving about two-fifths of metropolitan France and the empire to the French government. It met in the spa town of Vichy, which had many hotels and was never officially declared the capital. On 10 July 1940 the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, lobbied with promises and threats by Pierre Laval and Raphaël Alibert, voted by 569 to 80 to give full powers to Pétain. The Constitutional Acts of 11 and 12 July made him head of the French State, and the name French Republic disappeared from official documents. Most French historians and all postwar French governments have held the vote illegal.
sections.socioeconomy:
In 1940 the government took direct control of all production, which was synchronized with German demands, and replaced free trade unions with compulsory state unions. The armistice made France pay the costs of the German occupation troops, and it is estimated that France provided 42% of all foreign aid to the German economy. Germany held about two million French prisoners of war, and a law of September 1942 in effect deported workers to Germany, where by August 1944 they were 15% of the labour force.

The Germans seized about 20% of French food production, and farm output fell by half for lack of fuel, fertilizer and workers. The rationing system was stringent and badly mismanaged: the official ration gave starvation-level diets of 1013 or fewer calories a day, and a large black market grew. The National Revolution promoted the patriarchal family, motherhood and traditional Catholicism; government agencies had to fire married women employees, and the media were tightly controlled and spread virulent antisemitism. Women of the Resistance fought beside men, and France gave women the vote in 1944.
sections.military:
The armistice allowed a small Armistice Army in the unoccupied zone, set at 3,768 officers, 15,072 non-commissioned officers and 75,360 men, all volunteers, without tanks and short of motor transport. The colonial forces still had nearly 150,000 men in the Mediterranean area. Vichy defended its empire against both sides. On 3 July 1940 the Royal Navy attacked a French fleet at Mers El Kébir. In September 1940 Vichy forces at Dakar drove off Operation Menace, and in the Franco-Thai War Thailand attacked Indochina.

British and Commonwealth forces, with Free French troops, took Syria and Lebanon in the five-week campaign that ended on 14 July 1941, and Madagascar from May to November 1942. When the Allies invaded French North Africa in Operation Torch on 8 November 1942, Vichy forces at first resisted, killing 479 Allied soldiers, before Admiral François Darlan ordered them to stop. Germany then occupied the south in Case Anton and disbanded the Armistice Army, and the French fleet was scuttled at Toulon on 27 November 1942. From 30 January 1943 the Milice, a paramilitary force under Joseph Darnand, fought the Resistance.
sections.governance:
The Constitutional Acts of July 1940 gave Pétain all legislative, judicial, administrative, executive and diplomatic powers and the right to name his successor. Pétain never promulgated a new constitution. Democratic liberties were suspended, the "crime of opinion" was restored, critics were arrested, and elective bodies were replaced by nominated ones. Five governments followed: Pierre Laval's first, Pierre-Étienne Flandin's of two months to February 1941, François Darlan's to April 1942, and Laval's again until August 1944.

The regime's programme, the Révolution nationale, sought an anti-modern counter-revolution against the republican tradition, and Pétain's radio speeches blamed France's defeat on the "decadence" of the Third Republic. Scholars disagree whether it was fascist: Stanley G. Payne called it rightist and authoritarian but never fascist, while Roger Griffin described it as para-fascist. Historians also reject the label of puppet state: Robert Paxton found it an autonomous government doing things Germany did not require. Technocrats such as Jean Bichelonne pushed reforms, and René Bousquet unified the police, some of which were kept after the war.
sections.impact:
As soon as it was established, the regime took measures of its own against "undesirables": Jews, immigrants, Freemasons, Communists, Romani, homosexuals and left-wing activists. Some 15,000 people, mostly Jews, were denaturalized. The Law on the status of Jews of 3 October 1940 excluded Jews from the administration, the armed forces, teaching, law, medicine and other professions, and the next day a law authorized the detention of foreign Jews. Internment camps such as Gurs and Drancy became transit camps for the Holocaust.

In the Vel' d'Hiv Roundup of 16 and 17 July 1942, French police under René Bousquet and Jean Leguay arrested 13,152 Jews, including 4,051 children, whom the Gestapo had not asked for, and sent them through Drancy to Auschwitz. About 25,000 French Jews and 50,000 foreign Jews were deported; according to Robert Paxton, 76,000 Jews were deported and died in the camps. Vichy enacted racial laws in North Africa too. In 1995 President Jacques Chirac made the first official admission that the French State had been complicit in the deportations, and in 2017 Emmanuel Macron said that "it was indeed France that organised" the roundup.
sections.decline:
The empire slipped away from 1940, as French Equatorial Africa, Cameroun and the Pacific colonies rallied to Charles de Gaulle's Free France. After the Allied landings in North Africa and the German occupation of the south in November 1942, Vichy kept only residual authority. The Allies landed in Normandy and Provence in 1944, and after the liberation of Paris on 25 August 1944 German forces took Pétain and his ministers to Sigmaringen. There Fernand de Brinon led a commission with little or no authority until French forces took the town in April 1945.

The Provisional Government's Ordinance of 9 August 1944 declared all of Vichy's constitutional acts void, and the Allies recognized de Gaulle's government on 23 October 1944. In the purges, as many as 10,000 people were executed without trial, by the estimate de Gaulle accepted, and the purge commissions condemned about 120,000. Pétain was sentenced to death for treason in 1945, a sentence de Gaulle commuted to life imprisonment; Brinon and Darnand were executed. Later trials convicted Paul Touvier in 1994 and Maurice Papon in 1998. The historian Henry Rousso called Vichy a "past that doesn't pass away".

summary: Vichy France was the authoritarian French State that Marshal Pétain headed after the defeat of 1940. Officially neutral but bound by the armistice, it collaborated with Nazi Germany, persecuted Jews and other "undesirables" and helped deport 76,000 Jews to their deaths. Its independence ended with the German occupation of November 1942, and it fell with the liberation in 1944.

pointDescs.1940: The armistice of 22 June leaves Vichy two-fifths of metropolitan France and the empire, and the vote of 10 July gives Pétain full powers.
pointDescs.1941: Darlan's government holds power, but Syria and Lebanon fall to British and Free French forces by 14 July.
pointDescs.1942: After the Allied landings in North Africa, Germany occupies the south, the Armistice Army is disbanded and the fleet is scuttled at Toulon.
pointDescs.1943: The Milice is created to fight the Resistance as Vichy's authority dwindles.
pointDescs.1944: Paris is liberated, the ministers are taken to Sigmaringen, and the Ordinance of 9 August voids Vichy's acts.

notes: The brief asks for 8-20 points; the state lasted only four years, so five yearly points are all the article's dates support without inventing turning points.
The article's reference lists are empty in the saved text, so references are [].
The 10,000 executions without trial is de Gaulle's figure as the article gives it; Pétainist circles claimed 100,000 and Robert Aron 40,000.
End year 1944 per the register; the Sigmaringen commission lasted into April 1945.
